Home » Opinion » Morocco’s SMEs Are Entering an AI Tool-Sprawl Phase

Morocco’s SMEs and AI. | Credit: MWN Design Team.

For the past two years, much of the conversation around artificial intelligence in business has focused on adoption. Should companies use generative AI? Which jobs will change? Which processes can be automated? How quickly should businesses move?

For many Moroccan small and medium-sized enterprises, however, another problem is beginning to emerge.

AI is increasingly being added to digital environments that were already fragmented.

A company may have one tool for its website, another for ecommerce, a CRM for customer relationships, an accounting platform, an email marketing system, several social media tools, analytics platforms, cloud storage and internal messaging applications.

Artificial intelligence rarely replaces this stack.

Instead, it often adds another layer to it.

A content team starts paying for an AI writing assistant. Customer service experiments with a chatbot. The sales team adopts an automated prospecting platform. Management begins using an AI meeting assistant. Someone introduces an image-generation tool. Another department subscribes to a different platform for data analysis or workflow automation.

Individually, each decision may appear rational.

Collectively, they can create a new form of digital fragmentation: AI tool sprawl.

The first phase of generative AI adoption was relatively simple. Employees experimented with freely available tools. They tested prompts, generated text, summarized documents, and explored possible uses.

The second phase is different. AI features are now embedded in software companies already use, while thousands of specialized AI products compete to solve individual business problems.

For an SME, many of these tools appear inexpensive. A monthly subscription of $20, $30, or $50 does not usually require a formal investment decision. That is precisely why accumulation can happen so easily.

One department chooses one application. Another chooses a competing one. Employees create personal accounts. Free trials become paid subscriptions. Tools that were originally introduced for experimentation gradually become part of daily operations.

Six months later, the company may no longer know exactly how many applications it is paying for, what information employees are uploading to them, or whether several tools are performing essentially the same function.

The direct financial cost is only part of the issue. The higher cost is organizational.

This challenge is particularly relevant to Morocco because the country’s SME digital transformation is still deepening.

The World Bank noted in its 2026 Morocco Economic Update that fewer than one in five Moroccan firms currently make intensive and integrated use of advanced digital technologies such as enterprise software, customer-management systems and e-commerce tools.

At the same time, Morocco is accelerating its digital and AI ambitions. The DigiTPME initiative launched in 2026 seeks to support the digital transformation of very small, small and medium-sized companies, which represent more than 95% of Morocco’s economic fabric.

The country’s AI strategy is also moving rapidly from discussion to implementation through the AI Made in Morocco roadmap and broader Digital Morocco 2030 agenda.

This creates an important opportunity. But it also means that many companies are effectively undergoing two transformations simultaneously.

They are still trying to integrate conventional digital systems while also being encouraged to adopt artificial intelligence. If those two transformations are managed separately, fragmentation becomes very likely.

The most significant consequence of tool sprawl is not the number of icons on an employee’s computer. It is the fragmentation of information. Imagine a Moroccan SME where customer information exists partly in a CRM, partly in WhatsApp conversations, partly in spreadsheets and partly in an e-commerce platform.

Marketing data sits somewhere else. Invoices are stored in accounting software. Product information may be spread across the website, PDFs, catalogues and employee computers.

Now artificial intelligence is introduced. An AI assistant can only work with the information it can access.

If a company’s information is incomplete, duplicated or contradictory across different systems, artificial intelligence does not automatically solve the problem. It can simply process fragmented information faster.

This matters because the quality of AI outputs increasingly depends on the quality, accessibility and governance of the underlying information.

Before asking which AI model to adopt, many SMEs may therefore need to ask a more basic question: Where is our business information, and which version of it should we trust?

Moroccan companies also operate in a linguistic environment that many global software products were not originally designed around.

A single business may communicate internally in French, serve customers in Arabic or Darija, maintain parts of its website in English, and use different languages depending on whether it is working locally, with Europe, or across Africa.

AI can potentially make this environment easier to manage. But only when systems understand the languages and context being used.

Morocco’s recent initiatives around locally relevant artificial intelligence illustrate how important this issue has become. Work the Ministry of Digital Transition and Mistral announced, for example, includes technologies designed to recognize Moroccan Darija and handle speech that shifts between Arabic, French and English.

For SMEs, multilingual capability is therefore not a cosmetic feature. It affects customer service, search, documentation, internal knowledge, e-commerce and automation.

A collection of AI tools that each handles these languages differently can create additional inconsistency rather than reducing it.

Tool proliferation is often discussed as a cost issue, which matters, particularly for SMEs with limited budgets.

But duplicated subscriptions are relatively easy to identify. The harder questions concern ownership and responsibility. Who decides which AI tools employees may use? Who evaluates whether customer or company data can safely be uploaded? Who checks whether two teams are paying for competing platforms? Who determines whether a tool that worked during a pilot should become part of the company’s permanent infrastructure? And who removes a tool when it is no longer useful?

Without clear answers, technology purchasing becomes decentralized by default.

This is not necessarily the case due to poor management. The speed of AI adoption simply makes traditional procurement processes difficult to apply, as employees can adopt a new AI application in minutes without involving an IT department or making a major investment.

The barrier to experimentation has collapsed. Governance has not always caught up.

The instinctive response to rapid technological change is often to collect capabilities.

If one platform is good for writing and another is better for images, while a third is stronger in automation and a fourth is better for analysis, why not use all of them?

Sometimes that is the correct decision. Specialized tools can outperform integrated platforms in important areas.

But every additional application also creates another account to manage, another integration to maintain, another subscription to justify, another location where information may be stored, and another workflow employees must learn.

Which combination of tools creates the simplest reliable operating system for this company?

For many SMEs, the competitive advantage may eventually come from using fewer tools more deeply rather than continually adding new ones.
